McDaniel reported seeing it again on 6 May, and a radio search party said they heard something in the brush. The case later became a textbook example of how scares spread through a community.
signs: Three legs and two short arms
Dog-like tracks with six toe pads

name: Nain Rouge
region: Detroit, Michigan
first: In print in Marie Hamlin's Legends of Le Détroit, 1883
summary: Detroit's red imp, said to appear before every disaster to hit the city.
body: The Nain Rouge, French for 'red dwarf', is a small, red-faced imp with a glittering eye and a grin full of sharp teeth, said to haunt Detroit. Seeing it is a warning that something bad is coming.

The story says Detroit's founder, Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac, struck the imp with his cane and lost his fortune. Tellers say it danced among the dead after the Battle of Bloody Run in 1763, was seen before the 1805 fire that burned the city, and was spotted by utility workers just before the 1967 riots. The legend first appeared in print in 1883, so how far back it really goes is unclear.
Since 2010 Detroiters have held the Marche du Nain Rouge each spring, a costumed parade that banishes the imp from the city for another year.
signs: A small red figure with a wide, toothy grin
Seen just before fires, riots or disasters

famous.name: Seen after the Battle of Bloody Run

name: Fresno Nightcrawlers
region: Fresno and Yosemite Lakes Park, California
first: Security camera footage from 2007
summary: Walking pairs of white legs caught on a Fresno security camera.
body: Fresno Nightcrawlers are white, legs-only figures seen on home security footage, often described as a pair of pants out for a walk. They seem to have a tiny head and body sitting directly on long legs, and tend to appear in pairs.

The first clip was recorded in south Fresno in 2007 and shown on Univision. More footage followed from Yosemite Lakes Park in 2011. The TV show Fact or Faked: Paranormal Files gave them their name and could not prove the footage was faked. Skeptic Brian Dunning calls them an urban legend nobody truly believes in, yet they have become a beloved Fresno mascot, with T-shirts, toys and murals.
signs: Two long white legs with almost no body
Usually seen in pairs on security cameras

name: Black-eyed children
region: Reported across the US and UK; first story from Abilene, Texas
first: A 1996 online post by Texas reporter Brian Bethel
summary: Pale children with solid black eyes who knock and insist on being let in.
body: Black-eyed children look like ordinary kids or teens, usually pale and oddly dressed, until you see their eyes, which are completely black with no whites. They knock on doors or tap on car windows late at night and ask, politely but insistently, to be let in to use the phone or get a ride. Witnesses say they feel a wave of dread they cannot explain.

The legend traces to 1996, when reporter Brian Bethel posted about two black-eyed boys who approached his car in Abilene, Texas. The story spread through ghost forums, TV shows and, in 2014, a burst of British tabloid front pages. Bethel still says the encounter happened.
Researchers have found no documented cases beyond friend-of-a-friend stories, and the tale fits a long line of 'don't let it in' folklore.
signs: Pale children with completely black eyes
habitat: Doorsteps and parked cars at night

name: Shadow people
region: Reported worldwide, often in bedrooms at night
first: Popularised on Coast to Coast AM radio in 2001
summary: Dark, human-shaped silhouettes seen at the edge of vision, including the infamous Hat Man.
body: Shadow people are dark, featureless human silhouettes seen in the corner of the eye, in doorways or standing at the foot of the bed. They are usually solid black, darker than the room around them, and dart away when looked at directly.

The idea took off after Coast to Coast AM devoted a show to them in April 2001 and invited listeners to send drawings. The best-known figure is the Hat Man, a tall shadow in a brimmed hat and sometimes a long coat, often reported during sleep paralysis.

Sleep researchers point out that sleep paralysis often brings vivid sensed presences and figures, and the Hat Man is also widely reported by people who take dangerous overdoses of the antihistamine diphenhydramine.
signs: A figure in a brimmed hat watching from the doorway
Being unable to move on waking

famous.name: Coast to Coast AM shadow people show

name: Spring-heeled Jack
region: London and southern England, later the Midlands and Liverpool
first: October 1837, in south London
summary: A fire-breathing, high-leaping figure who terrorised Victorian England.
body: Spring-heeled Jack was a figure of Victorian panic: a tall, thin man in a black cloak with clawed hands and glowing red eyes, who could leap over walls and hedges in a single bound and breathed out blue and white flames.

Reports began in London in 1837. In January 1838 the Lord Mayor of London read out a letter about the attacks at a public session. On 19 February 1838, 18-year-old Jane Alsop answered her door to a man who said he was a policeman, then threw off his cloak, spat flames in her face and tore at her with claws. Lucy Scales reported a similar attack days later.
Sightings went on for decades, including sentries at Aldershot army camp in 1877, until the last widely reported appearance in Liverpool in 1904. He became a star of penny dreadful comics.
signs: Enormous leaps over walls and rooftops
Blue or white flames from the mouth
A cloak and tight-fitting oilskin suit

name: Popobawa
region: Pemba and Unguja islands, Zanzibar, and the Tanzanian coast
first: Pemba, around 1965
summary: A shape-shifting night spirit whose name means 'bat wing', behind waves of panic in Zanzibar.
body: Popobawa is a spirit from Zanzibar whose Swahili name means 'bat wing', after the shadow it is said to cast. It is a shapeshifter that can appear as a man or an animal, though it is often pictured as a small, one-eyed creature with bat wings. It visits homes at night, attacks sleepers, and brings a sulfur smell.

Reports began on Pemba around 1965 and returned in waves. In 1995 a major panic spread across Zanzibar and the coast to Dar es Salaam, with families sleeping outdoors around fires to avoid it. Shorter outbreaks followed in 2000 and 2007.
Researchers describe the waves as social panics tied to sleep paralysis, rumour and times of political tension.

name: Wendigo
region: Northern forests of Canada and the Great Lakes, in the traditions of Algonquian-speaking peoples
first: In English accounts since at least 1714; popularised by Algernon Blackwood's 1910 story
summary: A being of winter and hunger from Algonquian traditions, far removed from its horror-movie image.
body: The wendigo belongs to the traditions of several Algonquian-speaking peoples, including the Ojibwe, Cree, Saulteaux, Naskapi and Innu. In these teachings it is tied to winter, cold and starvation, and to greed that can never be satisfied. Ojibwe scholar Basil Johnston described it as gaunt, ash-grey and always hungry. It is also a moral idea, a warning about what selfishness does to a person and a community.
These are living spiritual traditions, and many Indigenous people prefer that the wendigo not be treated as a casual campfire monster. We keep this page short for that reason.

The antlered, deer-skulled 'wendigo' seen in films, games and online stories is a recent pop-culture invention that grew from Algernon Blackwood's 1910 story The Wendigo. Most modern 'wendigo sightings' online describe that version, not the being of the traditions.
signs: Modern reports describe a tall, gaunt figure in winter woods
Bitter cold and a sense of dread
Voices or calls deep in the forest

name: Thetis Lake Monster
region: Thetis Lake, near Victoria, British Columbia
first: August 1972
summary: A silver, scaly gill-man two teenagers said chased them from a BC beach in 1972.
body: On 22 August 1972, the Victoria Daily Times reported that two teenage boys said a silver-scaled, man-shaped creature with claws and a sharp, spiked head rose out of Thetis Lake and chased them off the beach. Two other boys fishing on the far shore said they saw it too. The RCMP investigated and found nothing.

Years later skeptic Daniel Loxton tracked down one of the witnesses, who admitted the story was made up. Loxton found the description matched the monster in Monster from the Surf, a film shown on local TV just days earlier.
signs: A pointed, spiked head with ear-like gills

name: Indrid Cold
region: Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia, and the Ohio Valley
first: 2 November 1966
summary: A smiling man in a shiny suit who stepped out of a UFO in West Virginia in 1966.
body: On the evening of 2 November 1966, salesman Woodrow Derenberger said a craft shaped like an old kerosene lamp blocked his truck on Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia. A tall man with dark slicked-back hair, a deep tan and a glossy coat stepped out, smiled, and spoke to him without moving his lips. He called himself Cold and said, 'We mean you no harm.'

Derenberger told the story on local TV the next day, and others came forward describing a similar grinning man. Writer John Keel folded the story into his Mothman Prophecies, and Indrid Cold became a fixture of Point Pleasant lore. Derenberger later claimed trips to Cold's home planet, Lanulos.
signs: A tall man with a fixed, too-wide grin
A lamp-shaped craft blocking the road

name: Grey aliens
region: Reported worldwide, especially in US abduction accounts
first: The 1961 Betty and Barney Hill case made the image famous
summary: Small, grey, big-headed beings with huge black eyes, the classic face of alien encounters.
body: Greys are the beings most often described in alien abduction and close encounter reports: short, slender, hairless humanoids with grey skin, an oversized head, tiny nose and mouth, and large, black, almond-shaped eyes. Tall versions are reported too.

Betty and Barney Hill's 1961 account of being taken aboard a craft in New Hampshire, recalled under hypnosis, set the template. Betty's sketch of a star map led to the idea that greys come from Zeta Reticuli. Later accounts of Roswell bodies and Whitley Strieber's 1987 book Communion, with its famous cover, made the face known everywhere.
Skeptics note that similar big-headed, big-eyed future humans appeared in science fiction long before 1961.
signs: Thin body and an oversized head
habitat: Inside craft, bedrooms and lonely roads

name: Nordic aliens
region: Mostly contactee reports from the US and Europe, especially in the 1950s
first: George Adamski said he met one in the California desert on 20 November 1952
summary: Tall, fair-haired, human-looking visitors from 1950s contactee stories.
body: Nordics are human-looking beings reported in UFO contact stories: tall, often 6 to 7 feet, with long fair hair, pale skin and light eyes. They are usually described as calm and kind, speaking telepathically and warning people about nuclear weapons or the health of the planet.

George Adamski said he met a long-haired visitor named Orthon near Desert Center, California in 1952, who told him he came from Venus. Other 1950s contactees reported similar 'space brothers', and from 1975 the Swiss farmer Billy Meier claimed contact with beings from the Pleiades.
Historians point to the 1951 film The Day the Earth Stood Still as one inspiration. From the 1960s on, greys largely replaced Nordics in encounter reports.
signs: Tall, human-looking people with long fair hair
habitat: Desert landing sites and contact meetings

name: Men in Black
region: Mostly the United States, following UFO sightings
first: Harold Dahl's 1947 Maury Island story; Albert K. Bender's 1953 visit
summary: Pale, oddly behaved men in black suits who warn UFO witnesses to keep quiet.
body: Men in Black are strangers in dark suits, hats and sunglasses who turn up after a UFO sighting and warn witnesses not to talk. Reports describe them as pale or oddly tanned, stiff, with flat voices, unfamiliar with everyday things like ballpoint pens, and arriving in old but brand-new-looking black cars.

In 1947 Harold Dahl claimed a man in a dark suit warned him about his Maury Island sighting. In 1953 Albert K. Bender shut down his UFO research group, saying three men in black had visited him. Author Gray Barker turned the story into a 1956 book, and John Keel reported MIB visits around Point Pleasant during the Mothman flap.
Folklorists compare them to old tales of meeting the devil on the road. The 1997 film made them comic heroes.
signs: Pale skin and stiff, odd movements
Knowing details they could not know
Old-model black cars that look new

name: Reptilians
region: Abduction reports worldwide; conspiracy theory spread online
first: Patrolman Herbert Schirmer's 1967 account from Ashland, Nebraska
summary: Scaly, reptile-like humanoids from some abduction reports, and a notorious conspiracy theory.
body: In UFO lore, reptilians are tall, scaly, reptile-like humanoids with slit-pupil eyes, described in a minority of abduction accounts. One of the earliest came from Ashland, Nebraska patrolman Herbert Schirmer, who under hypnosis recalled being taken aboard a craft in 1967 by beings with a slightly reptilian look and a winged-serpent emblem.

From the 1990s the idea was spun into a conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly rule the world. Researchers have traced it to pulp fiction of the 1920s, and note it often recycles old antisemitic tropes. This page is about encounter reports only.

name: Wampus cat
region: Appalachia, the Ozarks, Tennessee and the Carolinas
first: Appalachian folklore; in newspapers by the 1930s
summary: An Appalachian monster cat with glowing eyes, sometimes said to have six legs.
body: The wampus cat is a big, dark cat of Appalachian and Ozark folklore with glowing green or yellow eyes and a scream like a cougar. Depending on who tells it, it is a spirit cat with strange powers, a six-legged cat that can run forever, or an amphibious panther that swims like a mink.

Some versions draw on older Cherokee stories, while others are plain lumber camp yarns. In the 1930s, newspapers in the North Carolina Piedmont blamed a wampus cat for killing livestock. Today it is a popular school mascot, from the Conway Wampus Cats in Arkansas to schools in Texas and Tennessee.
signs: A dark cat bigger than a panther
Screams and whistles in the woods at night
size: 7 to 20 ft long in tall tales

famous.name: Knoxville paper describes a 15- to 20-foot wampus cat

name: Hodag
region: Rhinelander, Oneida County, Wisconsin
first: Newspaper reports in 1893
summary: Wisconsin's grinning, horned, spiny-backed beast of the logging camps.
body: The hodag is a fearsome critter of the northern Wisconsin logging camps: a dark beast with bull horns, a frog's head, a huge grin full of teeth, a row of spikes along its back and a spear-tipped tail. Lumberjacks said it was born from the ashes of mistreated oxen.

In 1893 surveyor and prankster Eugene Shepard announced that he and some locals had killed a hodag in Rhinelander with dynamite, and released a photo of its charred remains. In 1896 he claimed to have caught one alive and displayed it in a dark tent at the county fair, moving it with wires. When scientists said they would come to see it, he admitted it was a wooden carving.
Rhinelander embraced the beast: its schools are the Hodags, a giant statue stands by the chamber of commerce, and the Hodag Country Festival is held each summer.
signs: Bull horns and a wide, toothy grin
A row of spikes down the back
A long tail with a spear tip
The smell of buzzard meat and skunk

famous.name: Live hodag shown at the fair

name: Tsuchinoko
region: Mountain villages across western Japan; famously Shimokitayama, Nara
first: A yokai in old folklore; a wave of sightings in the late 1980s
summary: A short, fat, jumping snake from Japan with a bounty on its head.
body: The tsuchinoko is a snake-like creature from Japanese folklore, 30 to 80 centimetres long with a fat middle like a beer bottle, a narrow tail and a viper's fangs. It is said to jump a metre or more, sometimes twice in a row, and in some legends it speaks, lies and likes sake. Some say it bites its tail and rolls like a wheel.

In the late 1980s it turned from yokai to cryptid after a burst of sightings. In 1988 the village of Shimokitayama in Nara Prefecture launched a Tsuchinoko Expedition with a reward of a million yen for a live capture. About 200 people joined, and nothing was found. Tsuchinoko hunts are still held as village festivals, and Shimokitayama opened a Tsuchinoko Park in 2023.
Herpetologists suggest it could be a mamushi or blue-tongued skink that has just eaten a big meal.
signs: Jumping leaps of a metre or more
habitat: Mountain forest and rice paddy edges

name: Hoop snake
region: Rural United States, Canada and Australia
first: Described in a 1784 travel letter
summary: A snake that grabs its tail in its mouth and rolls after you like a wheel.
body: The hoop snake is a staple of American rural tall tales: a snake that takes its tail in its jaws and rolls downhill after its victim like a wagon hoop. At the last moment it straightens out and strikes with a venomous stinger on its tail. The only escape is to jump behind a tree, which takes the hit and dies.

A 1784 travel account from the United States described the rolling snake in detail, and the story later fed into Pecos Bill tales. Snake experts suggest the mud snake and rainbow snake, which have pointed but harmless tail tips, and the habit of some snakes of coiling in a loop.
signs: A snake rolling along in a hoop
A tree that withers after being struck

name: Mapinguari
region: Brazilian Amazon, especially Acre, Amazonas and Pará
first: Brazilian folklore; researched by ornithologist David Oren from the 1990s
summary: A foul-smelling Amazon giant, sometimes said to have a mouth on its belly.
body: The Mapinguari is a large, shaggy, upright creature of Amazon folklore, said to stink so badly it dizzies hunters. Folklore gives it backward-turned feet, hooked claws, a single eye and, most strangely, a gaping mouth in its belly. Its roar is said to sound like a human scream or thunder.

Ornithologist David Oren, of the Goeldi Museum in Belém, spent years interviewing rubber tappers, miners and Indigenous people who said they had seen or even shot one. He proposed that the stories could describe a surviving giant ground sloth, a group that died out about 10,000 years ago. His field searches found no animal, and most scientists remain doubtful.
signs: Twisted palm trees with the hearts eaten

name: Montauk Monster
region: Ditch Plains beach, Montauk, Long Island, New York
first: Found on 12 July 2008; reported on 23 July 2008
summary: A beaked, hairless carcass on a Long Island beach that broke the internet in 2008.
body: In July 2008, four friends found a strange, bloated carcass on Ditch Plains beach in Montauk, New York. It was hairless, with a beak-like face, sharp teeth and long-fingered paws. A local paper ran the photo as 'The Hound of Bonacville', blogs picked it up, and within days it was a worldwide story.

Rumours linked it to the Plum Island Animal Disease Center just offshore. The carcass vanished before scientists could examine it, but experts who studied the photos concluded it was most likely a raccoon that had been in the water for a while, with its upper jaw bones exposed. Similar 'monsters' have washed up on Long Island and elsewhere since.
size: About the size of a small dog

name: Sheepsquatch
region: Kanawha, Boone, Putnam and Mason counties, West Virginia
first: A "White Thing" tale in a 1965 folklore collection; sightings in the mid-1990s
summary: A woolly white, horned beast reported in West Virginia hollows in the 1990s.
body: Sheepsquatch is a West Virginia cryptid described as a bear-sized animal covered in long, shaggy white wool, with a sheep- or goat-like head, horns, and the ability to walk on four legs or stand upright. Witnesses also mention a sulfur smell and a scream like a woman.

Mountain folklore had stories of a 'White Thing' long before the name existed, including one in a 1965 collection about a woman who met a white beast riding home from church. A run of sightings in the mid-1990s, many around the Kanawha Valley near Cross Lanes, gave the creature its modern nickname.
signs: Walking on two legs or four

name: Cigar-shaped UFO
region: Worldwide
first: Reported since the late 1940s
summary: Long, wingless cylinders, sometimes glowing, sometimes releasing smaller objects.
body: Cigar- or cylinder-shaped UFOs are long, rounded, wingless objects, often metallic by day and glowing by night, sometimes with a row of lit 'windows'. Some witnesses say smaller discs or lights flew out of them, which earned them the nickname 'motherships'.

On 24 July 1948, Eastern Air Lines pilots Clarence Chiles and John Whitted said a glowing, wingless, cigar-shaped craft with two rows of lit windows shot past their DC-3 near Montgomery, Alabama, then pulled up into the clouds. It was one of the cases that convinced Air Force investigators at the time that UFOs deserved study, though Project Blue Book later put it down to a bright meteor. Contactee George Adamski claimed he saw a giant cigar-shaped 'mother ship' over Palomar, California in 1946 and photographed it the next year.
Many cylinder sightings turn out to be blimps, aircraft seen end-on in glare, or rocket and satellite re-entries.
signs: A row of lit windows or portholes
size: From tens of feet to hundreds of feet long

name: Boomerang and V-shaped UFOs
region: Worldwide; famous waves over New York and Arizona
first: The 1951 Lubbock Lights are an early example
summary: Huge V-shaped or chevron formations of lights, gliding silently overhead.
body: Boomerang UFOs are V-shaped or chevron-shaped objects, or formations of lights in a V, often described as enormous, silent and slow. Witnesses often cannot tell whether they are seeing one dark craft with lights on its edges, or separate lights moving together.

In 1951 residents and college professors in Lubbock, Texas saw a V of glowing lights cross the night sky several times. From 1983 to 1984 thousands of people in New York's Hudson Valley and western Connecticut reported a football-field-sized boomerang of coloured lights. Police later found that pilots in light Cessnas were flying in tight formation as a prank, though some witnesses insist that wasn't what they saw. On 13 March 1997 the Phoenix Lights, a mile-wide V of lights, crossed Arizona in front of thousands.
Formations of birds lit by streetlights, aircraft in formation and military flares explain many cases.
signs: Lights arranged in a V or chevron
A dark shape between the lights blocking stars

name: Ghost rockets
region: Sweden, Finland and the rest of Scandinavia
first: 26 February 1946, by Finnish observers
summary: Rocket-shaped objects that streaked across Scandinavian skies in 1946.
body: In 1946, a year before the term 'flying saucer' existed, people across Sweden and Finland began reporting rocket- or cigar-shaped objects streaking through the sky, some trailing fire, some apparently changing course. About 2,000 reports were logged between May and December, with peaks on 9 and 11 August.

On 19 July 1946 a farmer saw an object crash into Lake Kölmjärv in northern Sweden, and the Swedish military searched the lake but found nothing. Officials feared the Soviets were test-firing captured German V-weapons, and the Swedish army told newspapers not to print exact locations.
Investigators concluded that many sightings were meteors, and the August peaks match the Perseid shower. But some reports, including radar returns and recovered fragments, were never fully explained.
signs: A cigar or rocket shape with a fiery tail

name: Mystery airships
region: Across the United States, starting in California
first: November 1896, over Sacramento, California
summary: Lit-up 'airships' reported across America years before anyone could build one.
body: From late 1896 to mid-1897, thousands of Americans reported airships in the night sky: large, cigar-shaped gas bags with lights, propellers, sometimes wings, and occasionally a crew who spoke to the people below. Reports started over Sacramento in November 1896 and spread east through Texas and the Midwest by spring 1897.

Newspapers of the era printed wild tales, including a story that an airship crashed into a windmill in Aurora, Texas in April 1897 and its pilot was buried in the town cemetery, and a Kansas farmer's claim that an airship lassoed one of his cows. Both are now widely seen as hoaxes. No airship capable of such flights existed yet.
The wave is seen as a forerunner of modern UFO reports, with each era seeing the future technology it imagined.
signs: A lit, cigar-shaped craft at night
habitat: Night skies over towns and farms

name: Green fireballs
region: New Mexico and the US Southwest, near Los Alamos and Sandia
first: Pilots reported them over New Mexico on 5 December 1948
summary: Bright green balls of fire over New Mexico's nuclear labs that the military investigated.
body: Starting in late 1948, pilots, scientists and security guards around New Mexico's atomic sites reported brilliant green fireballs crossing the sky. They looked like meteors but were described as flying flat and level, burning a vivid green, and making no sound.

Meteor expert Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico saw one himself and said it did not behave like an ordinary meteor. The Army worried about foreign weapons, and in 1949 scientists including Edward Teller met at Los Alamos to discuss them. The Air Force ran Project Twinkle to photograph them, with little result.
Today most researchers think they were unusually bright bolide meteors, which can glow green from burning metals.
signs: A bright green ball of light
Breaking into fragments at the end

name: UFO crashes
region: Worldwide; best known in New Mexico, Pennsylvania and Nova Scotia
first: The Roswell debris recovery in July 1947
summary: Stories of objects falling from the sky and being quietly taken away.
body: Crash stories are some of the most famous in ufology: something falls from the sky, the military seals off the area, and witnesses say the debris, or bodies, were taken away in secret.

In July 1947 the Roswell Army Air Field announced it had recovered a 'flying disc' on a ranch in New Mexico, then said it was a weather balloon. In the 1990s the Air Force said it was debris from Project Mogul, a secret balloon program. On 9 December 1965 a fireball came down near Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, and residents described an acorn-shaped object hauled away by soldiers. On 4 October 1967 witnesses at Shag Harbour, Nova Scotia saw a lit object hit the sea, and the RCMP and navy searched the water.
Explanations include balloons, meteors and space debris. Each case still has dedicated researchers.
signs: A bright object falling from the sky

name: Alien abduction
aliases: Close encounter of the fourth kind
region: Reported worldwide, most often in North America
first: Antônio Villas Boas in Brazil in 1957 and the Hills in New Hampshire in 1961
summary: People who say they were taken aboard a craft, often remembering only 'missing time'.
body: Alien abduction reports describe being taken, usually at night from a bedroom or a lonely road, by beings into a craft, examined, and returned with gaps in memory. Common details include a bright light, paralysis, small grey beings, a medical-style exam and an hour or more of missing time.

Brazilian farmer Antônio Villas Boas told of a 1957 abduction, and Betty and Barney Hill's 1961 account from New Hampshire, recalled under hypnosis, became the template. In October 1973 two shipyard workers in Pascagoula, Mississippi, said they were taken aboard a craft by the river. In November 1975 Arizona logger Travis Walton disappeared for five days after his crew said a beam of light struck him.
Psychologists link many reports to sleep paralysis, false memories formed under hypnosis and cultural expectations. Abductees say their experiences are real.
signs: An hour or more of missing time
Grey beings and an exam table

name: Crop circles
region: Mostly southern England, especially Wiltshire; also worldwide
first: The term spread in the early 1980s; 1966 "saucer nests" in Australia
summary: Patterns flattened into fields overnight, long linked to UFOs.
body: Crop circles are patterns of flattened grain that appear in fields, often overnight, from simple circles to vast fractal designs. They cluster in southern England, especially Wiltshire near Avebury and Stonehenge, and became linked to UFOs and mysterious energies.

In 1966 a banana farmer at Tully, Queensland said he saw a saucer rise from a swamp and leave a flattened circular 'nest' in the reeds. Circles multiplied in England through the 1980s. In 1991 two men, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley, revealed they had been making circles since 1978 with a plank, rope and a wire loop on a cap to keep their lines straight, and showed reporters how.

Since then artist teams have openly made ever more complex formations, such as the 409-circle design at Milk Hill in 2001. All tested circles have been consistent with human makers, though some visitors still report odd lights and feelings in them.
signs: Flattened crop in precise geometric patterns
size: Tens to hundreds of feet across

famous.name: Bower and Chorley reveal their method

name: Cattle mutilations
region: Western United States, especially Colorado, New Mexico and the Plains
first: The death of a horse named Snippy in September 1967
summary: Cattle found dead with neat cuts and no blood, often blamed on UFOs.
body: Cattle mutilation reports describe livestock found dead with parts removed, such as an eye, an ear, the tongue or sex organs, with clean-looking cuts, little blood, and no tracks around the body. Ranchers sometimes reported lights or unmarked helicopters nearby.

The modern story began in September 1967 when a horse called Snippy was found near Alamosa, Colorado with the flesh stripped from its head and neck. Reports surged across the West in the 1970s. In 1979 a federal grant paid for an investigation in New Mexico led by retired FBI agent Kenneth Rommel. His 1980 report concluded that the cases were consistent with normal predators and scavengers.
Veterinarians explain the clean 'surgical' cuts as the work of birds, insects and decomposition. Theories have also blamed cults, secret government projects and the chupacabra.
signs: A carcass with eyes, tongue or ears removed
Little or no blood on the ground

name: Skinwalker Ranch
region: Near Ballard, Uintah Basin, north-eastern Utah
first: The Sherman family's story appeared in the Deseret News in 1996
summary: A Utah ranch famous for claims of UFOs, orbs, strange animals and cattle mutilations.
body: Skinwalker Ranch is a roughly 512-acre property in Utah's Uintah Basin, an area with UFO reports going back to the 1970s. In 1996 the Sherman family told the Deseret News of glowing orbs, mutilated cattle, a huge wolf that bullets could not hurt, and lights in the sky.

That year businessman Robert Bigelow bought the ranch for his National Institute for Discovery Science, and researchers logged around 100 odd incidents. The Defense Intelligence Agency later funded related work through a program called AAWSAP. Today the ranch is the setting of a TV series.

The name comes from the skin-walker of Navajo tradition. Navajo people generally do not discuss skin-walkers with outsiders and many object to the casual use of the word, so this page covers only the ranch.
